items.title: Per migliorare la qualità dell’aria che respiriamo serve aumentare la presenza della natura in città
items.description:
Il commento ai dati presentati oggi da Copernicus, che mostrano quanto il problema delle emissioni inquinanti sia globale
The post Per migliorare la
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie La qualità dell’aria è una delle dimensioni più concrete attraverso cui la crisi ambientale entra nella vita quotidiana delle persone. E per tutelarla servono misure concrete, come una drastica riduzione delle  emissioni di inquinanti atmosferici e di gas serra e l’aumento degli spazi verdi in città. Il WWF Italia commenta così i dati presentati oggi dal Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), che mostrano quanto il problema delle emissioni inquinanti sia globale e quanto il cambiamento climatico possa contribuire a modificarne intensità e diffusione. La complicità delle ondate di caldo Nei primi otto mesi del 2026, appena il 5% della popolazione mondiale ha respirato livelli di ozono classificati come “Good”, cioè entro le linee guida dell’Organizzazione Mondiale della Sanità. Al contrario, quasi il 40% della popolazione mondiale è stata esposta a livelli classificati come “Poor”, “Very Poor” o “Extremely Poor”. In Europa, nello stesso periodo, il 50% della popolazione è stato esposto a una di queste tre categorie di qualità dell’aria per l’ozono. È un dato particolarmente significativo perché l’ozono troposferico è un inquinante secondario: non nasce direttamente dalle emissioni, ma si forma in atmosfera attraverso reazioni chimiche che coinvolgono altri inquinanti, favorite dalla radiazione solare e dalle temperature elevate. Le ondate di calore possono quindi contribuire ad aggravare l’inquinamento da ozono, rendendo sempre più evidente l’interconnessione tra cambiamento climatico e qualità dell’aria. Il pericolo per la salute umana Lo stesso ozono troposferico è inoltre un gas serra, aggiungendo un ulteriore elemento alla complessa relazione tra atmosfera, clima e inquinamento. La complessità dell’ozono rende inoltre evidente che la qualità dell’aria non può essere affrontata soltanto su scala locale: gli inquinanti precursori possono essere trasportati a distanza e le condizioni atmosferiche ne influenzano formazione e distribuzione. La dimensione sanitaria rende ancora più evidente la portata del problema. Secondo l’Organizzazione Mondiale della Sanità, il 99% della popolazione mondiale vive in luoghi in cui la qualità dell’aria non rispetta le linee guida OMS e l’inquinamento atmosferico ambientale è associato a oltre 4 milioni di morti premature ogni anno. Gli effetti dell’inquinamento non riguardano soltanto l’apparato respiratorio e cardiovascolare: le evidenze scientifiche mostrano conseguenze su numerosi organi e sistemi dell’organismo. L’importanza del verde urbano In questo scenario, la natura nelle città può rappresentare una parte importante della risposta. Il verde urbano non sostituisce le politiche necessarie a ridurre le emissioni alla fonte e non può essere considerato una soluzione automatica all’inquinamento atmosferico. Ma alberi, arbusti, prati e altri spazi verdi, se progettati in modo adeguato al contesto, possono contribuire a migliorare la qualità dell’aria attraverso l’intercettazione di parte del particolato e di alcuni inquinanti, oltre a mitigare le temperature locali e l’effetto isola di calore grazie all’ombreggiamento e all’evapotraspirazione. Per questo il verde urbano non dovrebbe essere considerato un elemento ornamentale, ma una vera infrastruttura della città. Un’infrastruttura che deve essere progettata tenendo insieme biodiversità, adattamento climatico, qualità dell’ambiente e salute delle persone, scegliendo specie, densità e configurazioni adeguate alle caratteristiche di ciascun luogo. Il ruolo di Urban Nature È questo l’obiettivo di Urban Nature, il festival WWF della natura in città che il 3 e 4 ottobre torna con la sua decima edizione: riportare la natura al centro della progettazione delle nostre città e riconoscerne il valore non solo per la biodiversità, ma anche per la qualità della vita delle persone. Di fronte a temperature sempre più elevate e a una qualità dell’aria che continua a rappresentare una delle principali pressioni ambientali sulla salute, avere più natura nelle città significa contribuire ad aumentare la capacità degli ambienti urbani di affrontare queste pressioni e, al tempo stesso, creare luoghi più vivibili, resilienti e salutari.  Urban nature 2026 Sabato 3 e Domenica 4 ottobre saremo presenti in più di 100 piazze italiane con i nostri stand  per raccontare il valore della Natura in città ai cittadini, attraverso la distribuzione del miele WWF, che aiuterà a creare il Fondo Spazi Natura WWF.  Vivi la tua città… Scopri di più

items.title: Committed Antarctic Ice Sheet mass loss by the end of the twenty-first century

Committed Antarctic Ice Sheet mass loss by the end of the twenty-first century
                        Yucheng Lin 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-5556-44901,2, Xuebin Zhang 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-1731-35242, Nicholas R. Golledge 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-7676-89703, Robert E. Kopp 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-4016-94284,5, John A. Church 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-7037-81946, Yi Jin 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0001-6415-93072, Chen Zhao

Nature Geoscience

            Save article
            
        
        
            
                View saved research

AbstractThe Antarctic Ice Sheet is the largest source of uncertainty in sea-level rise projections, with uncertainties propagating through emissions scenarios, atmosphere–ocean general circulation models, ice-sheet dynamics and sea-level physics. In ice-sheet model intercomparison exercises, these uncertainties—typically attributed to intermodel differences—stem from modelling choices that may bias ensembles towards commonly adopted approaches regardless of observational consistency. Here we quantify how each individual physical assumption cascades into projection uncertainty using a machine-learning emulation framework, which also enables Bayesian calibration against satellite observations to reduce projection bias. Our results suggest it is very likely (≥0.92 probability) that the Antarctic Ice Sheet is committed to twenty-first-century mass loss, even under aggressive emissions-reduction scenarios. Higher emissions drive greater Antarctic mass loss by 2100 (≥0.89 probability), directly elevating near-term coastal risks. Under very high-emissions scenarios, we identify cascading mechanisms that could produce up to 25.4 cm of sea-level rise by 2100 (95th percentile; median = 15.7 cm) while remaining consistent with satellite observations. Effective management of these risks to densely populated coastal communities requires rapid emissions reductions and improved constraints on climate model selection, sliding laws and ice-shelf melt parameterizations.

                            Climate and Earth system modelling

                            Coastal Resilience and Adaptation to Sea Level Rise

MainSea-level rise (SLR) has intensified coastal hazards over recent decades1—a trend projected to accelerate this century—posing substantial socio-economic risks to densely populated coastal communities2,3. The Antarctic Ice Sheet (AIS) contains Earth’s largest freshwater reservoir, equivalent to 57.9 m of global mean SLR. Although AIS mass loss accounted for ~10% of global mean SLR over 2006–20183, its large volume means it dominates the uncertainty in future SLR projections4.Contemporary AIS projections rely on ice-sheet models that simulate large-scale ice dynamics in response to climate forcing, capturing self-sustained AIS evolution5. Implementing such models necessitates several modelling decisions (Fig. 1), such as climate forcing, physical assumptions of ice-dynamical processes and model initialization methods (Extended Data Table 1)5,6. These modelling choices fundamentally drive divergent AIS projections: they vary markedly among studies, reflecting different interpretations of complex physics informed by diverse observations3. Currently, limited understanding and computational capacity hinder definitive evaluation of these choices, perpetuating large SLR projection uncertainty. This is highlighted by the Ice Sheet Model Intercomparison Project (ISMIP6) for the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6)5,6,7, where 2100 AIS projections under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) 5–8.5 span <−7 to >40 cm of sea-level equivalent (SLE)5, with non-participating models suggesting an even broader range8.Fig. 1: Uncertainty cascade in AIS sea-level rise projections.Full size imageThis sequential modelling framework illustrates the information chain from emissions scenarios through coupled earth system models to AIS numerical models and spatio-temporally variable sea-level projections. Emissions scenarios drive coupled atmosphere–ocean general circulation models (AOGCMs) that simulate interactions between Earth system components (such as ocean dynamics, atmospheric dynamics and sea ice) to produce a global signal—global mean surface temperature (GMST) change—and a regional oceanic and atmospheric signal representing Antarctic conditions. These signals force numerical ice-sheet models by providing surface mass balance and a regional ocean signal that drives ice-shelf melt parameterizations to translate ocean warming outside the ice-shelf cavity into basal melt beneath the ice shelves, thereby driving ice-shelf thinning and grounding-line migration. The resulting ice dynamics are further governed by additional modelling choices, including sliding laws, ice-shelf melt parameterization schemes and ice-shelf collapse mechanisms. The modelling chain culminates in spatio-temporally variable relative sea-level rise projections, accounting for gravitational, rotational and deformational effects. Coloured text indicates emulatable variables in this study: red (GMST, with optional emissions scenario dependence), orange (CMIP AOGCM choices), blue (ice-modelling features) and cyan (relative sea-level change). More details about model features are described in Extended Data Table 1. Sea-level change and coupled AOGCM basemaps generated using Cartopy47 with data from Natural Earth (https://naturalearthdata.com). Global warming stripes graphic adapted from #ShowYourStripes under a Creative Commons license CC BY 4.0.Ice-sheet model intercomparison projects5,6,9 and individual modelling studies10,11,12 have advanced understanding of ice-sheet dynamics over recent decades. However, critical challenges remain. First, intercomparison ensemble projections follow a ‘one model, one vote’ approach that can bias results towards modelling choices adopted by more groups, regardless of physical plausibility or historical performance13,14. Second, different ice-sheet model results are broadly attributed to intermodel differences15, and how each modelling choice impacts projections has not been systematically investigated. Third, AIS uncertainties in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Assessment Reports3,16 reflect cascading effects from external forcing through to ice-model assumptions, which are often obscured in communication and may lead to overinterpretation of instability mechanisms without considering their dependence on other modelling choices. Finally, the lengthy timeframes required to assess alternative ice-model parameters hinder timely integration of evolving uncertainty into coastal adaptation planning17.To improve these limitations, we use ISMIP6-23005 to train a machine-learning emulation framework that links physical assumptions to global mean and location-specific SLR projections with uncertainty quantification (Methods). These assumptions include Atmosphere–Ocean General Circulation Model (AOGCM) choice, global mean surface temperature (GMST) and various ice-model assumptions. We restrict the emulation to 2100, as the ensemble is too small to capture the strong nonlinearities emerging from the twenty-second century onward. The emulator performs robustly under tenfold cross validation across prediction targets (Methods, Extended Data Figs. 1–3 and Extended Data Table 2), enabling probabilistic SLR projections with flexible model assumptions. This enables investigation of spatio-temporally variable SLR projection uncertainty structures that arise from each modelling assumption within ISMIP66, informing future experiment design. Furthermore, a Bayesian calibration framework is developed to reduce AIS projection bias using satellite observations.Quantifying cascading uncertainties in AIS-induced SLRWe quantified how GMST (relative to 2015), AOGCM, and ice-sheet model features impact SLR projection uncertainty using a Bayesian hierarchical framework (Methods). Given the difficulty in distinguishing which ice-model parameters are more realistic3, we adopt a uniform prior that assumes all ISMIP6 ice-model options are equally plausible (for example, different sliding laws) and that GMST warming levels are uniformly distributed between no further warming since 2015 and the maximum CMIP AOGCM output at each time step. On the basis of these priors, we generated a large ensemble to estimate each feature’s contribution to overall SLR projection variance (Methods).AIS projections rely on either raw or drift-corrected simulations. Raw simulations directly use ice-model outputs that capture nonlinear ice dynamics and are employed by most individual studies10,11,12. However, many raw simulations do not reproduce observed mass-loss trends or exhibit unrealistic model drift14. Intercomparison projects therefore often employ drift-corrected simulations (raw simulations minus control runs) to isolate ice-sheet dynamical responses to climate change while removing systematic biases6,7. However, drift-corrected simulations cannot fully preserve nonlinear ice-sheet dynamics7, limiting SLR projection credibility. We therefore investigated uncertainty structures for both simulation types. For drift-corrected simulations, we followed the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) approach3 by adding a 0.33 ± 0.16 mm yr−1 (1σ) linear trend to account for background AIS mass loss removed in the control runs, assuming it is independent of other model features.Our results show that ice-model features dominate twenty-first-century AIS uncertainty in raw simulations, averaging 64%. Before 2030, emulator-predictive uncertainty (from the emulator’s imperfect approximation of ice-sheet model) dominates due to overall low projection uncertainty (Fig. 2a,b). Sliding laws, which relate basal shear stress to basal sliding velocity and influence ice-sheet flow18, account for 21% of variance over 2015–2100. As current CMIP AOGCMs provide only marginal ocean warming signals without resolving ice-shelf cavities, ice-shelf melt parameterizations translate this warming into spatially variable ice-shelf basal melt rates19, contributing 20% of variance. Partial-dependence analysis, which quantifies the expected SLR for specific modelling options averaged over many combinations of the other features (Methods), reveals that a Budd-type sliding law20 yields 5.0 ± 4.2 cm higher SLR in 2100 than a linear Weertman law21. Ice-shelf melt parameterizations have a similar impact: an observation-calibrated linear thermal forcing function12 yields 7.8 ± 5.2 cm more than ISMIP6 standard non-local parameterization22.Fig. 2: The impact of ice-modelling choice on AIS SLR projection uncertainties.Full size imagea–j, Results for raw-simulation scenario (a–e) and drift-corrected simulation scenario (raw simulations minus control runs) (f–j), respectively. Drift-corrected simulation scenario incorporates a historical mass-loss trend of 0.33 ± 0.16 mm yr−1 (ref. 3). a,f, Percentage contribution of different modelling choices to the sum of expected feature-induced variance (Methods), shown with 15-year moving averages. Colour legend is given in b, where numerical uncertainty aggregates contributions from numerics, stress balance, varying resolution and highest spatial resolution choices, with highest spatial resolution being the predominant uncertainty source. Others indicate uncertainties from all other ice-modelling choices such as ice flow model and geothermal heat (Extended Data Table 1). b,g, One standard deviation uncertainty contribution by each feature, following the same colour scheme as in a and f. c,h, Partial dependence of SLR on ice-shelf melt parameterization choice. d,i, Partial dependence of SLR on the sliding law choice. e,j, Partial dependence of SLR on the CMIP AOGCM choice. Note we do not show partial-dependence uncertainty here for better visual clarity. GMST = global mean surface temperature; DEM = digital elevation model; Lin = observation-constrained linear thermal forcing function12; PICO = Potsdam Ice-shelf Cavity mOdel48; Quad. non-local = ISMIP6 standard non-local quadratic parameterizations22.Numerical implementation schemes are another major uncertainty source. Model spatial resolution contributes 8% of variance (Fig. 2a,b) by determining the model’s ability to resolve fine-scale topography that controls ice-stream dynamics and grounding-line processes23. Adopting 1-km resolution yields 4.3 ± 2.8 cm less SLR than 8-km resolution (Extended Data Fig. 4). Different treatments of ocean-driven ice-shelf basal melt in partially floating cells at grounding zones contribute 6% of variance. Although no model includes Marine Ice Cliff Instability (MICI)24, ISMIP6 incorporates a simplified ice-shelf collapse scheme5, contributing negligibly early in the century but growing to 5% of variance by 2100, with activated collapse adding 2.8 ± 1.4 cm of SLR. Other identifiable contributors include initialization year (5%) and bedrock digital elevation model (1%; Extended Data Fig. 4).Climate forcing components contribute moderately to twenty-first-century variance in raw simulations: 9% for AOGCMs and 6% for GMST. GMST reflects global-scale warming, whereas AOGCMs determine regional departures from the global average, which translate into Antarctic surface mass balance and regional ocean warming signals fed into ice-sheet models5,6 (Fig. 1). Early in the twenty-first century, both GMST and AOGCM variations remain small relative to 2015 conditions but increase as higher emissions scenarios drive greater divergence, contributing 12% and 14% variance by 2100, respectively.Drift-corrected simulations exhibit a different uncertainty structure, with substantially lower variance (Fig. 2b,g). This reduction occurs because control run variability—45% of raw-simulation variance—is replaced by a linear historical trend. Control runs contain variability from ice-model features, not from climate forcing or ice-shelf collapse5 (Extended Data Fig. 5). Removing this component reduces ice-model feature uncertainty to 23% during 2015–2100. In contrast, climate forcing and ice-shelf collapse uncertainties remain identical between simulation types. Consequently, climate forcing components dominate the uncertainty structure, contributing nearly half of twenty-first-century variance (31% from AOGCMs, 17% from GMST). Historical trend uncertainty is also important, peaking at 30–33% of variance in 2030–2040.In drift-corrected simulations, ice-model feature uncertainties reflect their interactions with climate forcing. Whereas sliding laws dominate raw-simulation uncertainties, they contribute 4% of twenty-first-century variance here, with a 0.3 ± 1.1 cm difference between Budd and linear Weertman laws in 2100 (Fig. 2i). This suggests sliding laws primarily contribute to historical trends and model drift rather than climate forcing interactions, possibly because large-scale marine ice-sheet instability remains untriggered in most simulations by 2100. Similarly, the contribution of ice-shelf melt parameterization decreases to 5%, and observation-calibrated linear thermal forcing produces 2.8 ± 2.5 cm more than ISMIP6 standard non-local parameterization. For both raw and drift-corrected simulations, our emulation is broadly consistent with independent numerical-model-based sensitivity analyses10,12,23, suggesting it robustly reproduces AIS dynamical behaviour (Supplementary Information).The spatial distribution of AIS mass change is another uncertainty source in regional sea-level projections. AIS mass variations trigger gravitational, rotational and deformational effects that produce spatially variable relative SLR patterns or sea-level fingerprints25,26. Identical total mass loss can yield distinct regional SLR depending on its spatial distribution. We quantify this with a pattern-matching post-processing procedure that links emulated SLE to spatially variable SLR, accounting for realistic mass-loss geometries (Supplementary Information). Combined with other uncertainties, this defines the location-dependent uncertainty structure (Fig. 3). Across six coastal megacities, it falls into three regimes. In London and Singapore, AIS mass-loss geometry contributes <1% of variance, reflecting a well-constrained local-to-global SLR ratio at these low-variance locations. New York and Shanghai are slightly more sensitive, at 5% and 3% of variance, mainly due to rotational effects26. Near the AIS, mass-loss geometry rivals ice-dynamic features as a major uncertainty source, reaching 17% in Buenos Aires and 21% in Melbourne.Fig. 3: Antarctic-induced spatially variable SLR and associated uncertainty structure in drift-corrected simulations.Full size imagea–h, Relative sea-level change at different cities (a–c,f–h; city names given in panel titles), with locations marked in d and e. White and black dashed lines indicate the ensemble-mean local relative sea-level and global mean sea-level change, respectively. Coloured shading indicates the 5th–95th percentile range (90% credible interval) of the relative sea-level projections. Sea-level change projection uncertainties are decomposed into components related to historical trends, emulator prediction, external forcing (GMST and AOGCM options), ice-dynamic features and sea-level fingerprints according to their temporally variable variance fractions. d, Ensemble-mean relative sea-level change map at 2100, with black dashed lines indicating contours of global mean sea-level rise. e, Sea-level fingerprint uncertainty contribution to overall variance due to uncertain AIS mass change geometry. Note that this uncertainty considers only normalized sea-level fingerprint uncertainty, which differs from overall sea-level fingerprint uncertainty that includes uncertain AIS mass variation magnitude. Maps in d and e generated using Cartopy47.The impact of external forcing on AIS evolutionAIS evolution is known to display a complex relationship with external forcing4,11. This relationship depends on ice-sheet modelling choices alongside AOGCM-derived surface mass balance and regional ocean warming trajectories under various emissions scenarios. Using the same prior assumptions, we assess AIS evolution as a function of GMST conditioned upon different AOGCMs (Methods). Considering many ISMIP6 raw simulations do not reproduce historical mass-loss trends7,27, introducing unrealistic noise, drift-corrected simulations provide a suitable framework for examining relative differences in ice-sheet responses to external forcing (compare with absolute differences in raw simulations; Table 1).Table 1 Antarctic-induced sea-level rise projections for 2100Full size tableThe relationship between twenty-first-century AIS-induced SLR and GMST is delayed, non-stationary and nonlinear (Fig. 4). The delay reflects the substantial forcing required to initiate AIS mass loss and the lag between climate perturbation and dynamical response, with the resulting mass loss potentially persisting for millennia28,29. With forcing applied from 2015, distinguishable SLR differences between SSPs emerge only in the late twenty-first century, whereas GMST differences appear much earlier. These SSP-specific GMST distributions are derived from a simple climate model (FaIR30; Methods). The relationship is also non-stationary: SLR uncertainty increases with both time and GMST (Fig. 4a–d). By 2100, 1σ uncertainty increases from 2.45 cm at 0–2 °C to 5.94 cm at 4.5–6 °C warming level, reflecting greater uncertainty in atmospheric and oceanic responses under high-emissions scenarios that propagates through the AIS dynamical system12.Fig. 4: Climate forcing impacts on AIS SLR projections and uncertainties in drift-corrected simulations.Full size imagea–d, Antarctic-induced SLR probability density functions at each quarter (as labelled in the panel titles) of the twenty-first century as a function of GMST change relative to 2015, assuming all other modelling options in ISMIP6 are equally plausible (Methods). Dashed coloured contours indicate 90% credible intervals of SSP-dependent GMST and SLR distributions. Grey dots indicate numerical simulation results from ISMIP65. Coloured boxes on the right of each panel represent SSP-dependent SLR distributions (n = 500,000): centre line, median; box bounds, 25th and 75th percentiles; whiskers, 5th and 95th percentiles; dots, tail samples outside the 5th–95th percentile range. e–i, Antarctic-induced SLR probability density functions at 2100 as a function of GMST change relative to 2015, conditioned on CMIP AOGCM options (where grey dots indicate ISMIP6 simulations under this AOGCM): UKESM (e), CESM2 (f), HadGEM2 (g), CCSM4 (h) and NorESM1-M (i). j, 2100 GMST distribution relative to 2015 conditioned on five SSPs, created by a simple climate model FaIR30,49. k, 2100 AIS SLR distributions corresponding to five SSPs. l, The probability of exceeding SSP1–1.9 sea-level rise under higher emissions scenarios with 15-year moving averages. Cases where two scenarios produce indistinguishable differences in SLR are excluded.Whereas the AIS’s delayed and non-stationary behaviour is well documented11,28, the reconstructed nonlinear SLR-GMST relationship remains AOGCM dependent. By 2100, AIS-induced SLR increases modestly at 0–2 °C (0.12 ± 0.01 cm °C−1) but substantially more at 2–4.5 °C (1.79 ± 0.01 cm °C−1; Fig. 4d). Over the twenty-first century, warmer atmosphere enhances snowfall and net mass gain31, whereas ocean warming generally correlates with ice mass loss3. Different AOGCMs exhibit varying atmospheric and oceanic warming around Antarctica, which do not always co-vary32, thereby complicating the SLR-GMST relationship. Among the tested AOGCMs, NorESM1-M, CCSM4, HadGEM2-ES and CESM2-WACCM show higher GMST and correspondingly increased SLR under high-emissions scenarios. UKESM1-0-LL reaches the highest twenty-first-century warming of any AOGCM yet produces a net mass gain from increased snowfall and modest regional ocean warming. Notably, this net mass gain is transient, confined to the twenty-first century before sustained ocean-driven dynamic losses overtake surface accumulation (Extended Data Fig. 6).IPCC AR6 acknowledged the uncertain twenty-first-century AIS scenario dependence, noting ‘low agreement on the relationship between emissions scenarios and AIS response’3. Using our variance-analysis methodology, we quantified the sensitivity of AIS response to ice-model features under SSP1–1.9 and SSP5–8.5. AOGCM choice is the dominant factor controlling scenario dependence, with HadGEM2 producing 58% higher positive-scenario dependence probability than UKESM (Table 1), whereas different ice-model options produce only up to 10–11% differences. This applies to both raw and drift-corrected simulations because an identical control run was used for different emissions scenarios. Therefore, while ice-model features act as nonlinear amplifiers of external forcing and contribute substantially to SLR variance, AOGCM choice exerts dominant control over net mass gain or loss by 2100. The probability of higher SLR under SSP5–8.5 than SSP1–1.9 increases rapidly between 2015 and 2040 (zero indicates initially negligible scenario divergence) and continues to rise through the late twenty-first century (Fig. 4l).Bayesian calibration and high-end SLR mechanismsDisagreement between raw ISMIP6 simulations and observations compromises SLR projection reliability. This necessitates drift-corrected simulations7,33, but they cannot fully capture nonlinear ice-sheet dynamics. A major limitation is that many raw simulations are initialized to fit static rather than transient observations such as time-dependent surface velocities27. Calibrating numerical models to transient observations can yield higher-fidelity projections but is computationally expensive34,35. Our emulation provides an intermediate approach by applying Bayesian calibration to update prior assumptions against time-dependent mass-loss observations, thereby deriving posterior parameter distributions and SLR projections (Methods).Bayesian calibration against the 2002–2021 AIS mass-loss rate (0.44 ± 0.04 mm yr−1 (ref. 36)) yields a 30–42% reduction in uncertainty (5th–95th percentile) and a 15–25% increase in median projections for raw simulations across SSPs (Fig. 5 and Table 1; uncertainty is similarly reduced in the 2300 projection experiments; Supplementary Information). These variations arise as observations update prior assumptions, yielding posterior probabilities that favour specific modelling options. For sliding laws—a major contributor to model drift and SLR uncertainty—observations disfavour pseudo-plastic (q = 0.3) and Budd formulations that produce unrealistically fast ice flow, favouring moderate formulations instead.Fig. 5: Antarctic contribution to future sea-level rise using different calibration schemes.Full size imagea, AIS SLR projections under SSP5–8.5 GMST variation using prior, posterior and posterior high-end physical parameter combinations (Methods). The inset demonstrates the calibration process of SLR projections under different schemes compared to the observed AIS mass-loss trend that excludes emulator-predictive uncertainty for better clarity, whereas the main figure incorporates full uncertainty quantification. All projections use raw simulations without subtracting control runs. Projections for each SSP and calibration scheme are available at Extended Data Fig. 7. b, SSP-dependent SLR distributions for prior, posterior (both n = 100,000) and posterior high-end (n = 10,000) calibration schemes: centre line, median; box bounds, 25th and 75th percentiles; whiskers, 5th and 95th percentiles; dots, tail samples outside the 5th–95th percentile range. c, Probability for each AOGCM option under prior, posterior and posterior high-end schemes. d–h, Same as c but for different physical features and options, labelled as panel titles and labels, respectively. The modelling choices shown here were implemented by at least two ISMIP6-2300 submissions5. Weertman (m = 1) is equivalent to linear Weertman. Lin = observation-constrained linear thermal forcing function12; PICO = Potsdam Ice-shelf Cavity mOdel48; Quad. local = ISMIP6 standard local quadratic parameterizations22; Quad. non-local = ISMIP6 standard non-local quadratic parameterizations22; Quad. non-local slope = ISMIP6 non-Local parameterization with slope dependence of the melt22; HO = higher order; SSA = shallow shelf approximation.Assimilating observational constraints increases the probability of twenty-first-century AIS mass loss. Under the posterior scheme, the AIS is very likely committed to continued mass loss by 2100 even under SSP1–1.9 (P = 0.92; 0.80 for prior), rising to ≥ 0.95 under SSP5–8.5 (0.85 for prior). Therefore, warming-enhanced snowfall is very unlikely to compensate for ocean-driven mass loss. This shift reflects higher posterior probabilities for modelling choices better reproducing recent AIS mass loss. HadGEM2 and NorESM, two AOGCMs with the highest positive-scenario-dependence probabilities, increase from 0.20 to 0.22 and 0.21, respectively (Fig. 5c), whereas UKESM, the only AOGCM favouring net mass gain, decreases to 0.18.Although short-term AIS mass-loss observations effectively constrain model drift, they weakly constrain processes that minimally affect recent mass-loss trends but may trigger substantial future mass loss. Except for sliding laws, posterior probabilities for most modelling choices remain strongly prior dependent. AIS evolution is subject to strong ambiguity—a type of deep uncertainty that cannot be adequately represented by single, well-defined probability distributions, necessitating exploring alternative priors to inform risk assessment8. Our emulator facilitates such assessment through probability boxes—an approach adopted by IPCC AR6 SLR projections3,37 (Supplementary Information). Furthermore, testing an alternative ISMIP6-main-submission prior confirms our key inferences remain robust (Supplementary Information).Another deep-uncertainty assessment involves characterizing unknown-likelihood, high-impact outcomes for risk-averse decision-makers8. We therefore analyse cascading mechanisms that produce physically plausible high-end SLR while remaining consistent with AIS observations. This posterior high-end scheme is defined as posterior parameter combinations producing the highest 1% of 2100 SLR under SSP5–8.5. This trajectory begins when a highly sensitive ocean warming response coincides with a highly sensitive ice-shelf melt parameterization that converts this warming into basal melt. When this enhanced basal melt is paired with a relatively strongly plastic sliding law, reduced basal resistance amplifies ice discharge, particularly under higher order stress-balance formulations. This intensifies when subgrid-scale melt and ice-shelf collapse activate, together reducing buttressing and enabling rapid grounding-line retreat, potentially triggering marine ice-sheet instability38. Together, these mechanisms form a plausible accelerated mass-loss pathway, yielding 15.7 cm (9.8–25.4 cm) of SLR by 2100.These cascading mechanisms collectively drive strong positive-scenario dependence (P ≥ 0.99). This effect is pronounced when GMST increases from SSP2–4.5 to SSP5–8.5 levels, yielding 2.0 (1.1–3.4) times higher SLR by 2100 (Fig. 5b), similar to simulations incorporating MICI11. This reflects a nonlinear increase of SLR with GMST in 2100, from 0.56 ± 0.01 cm °C−1 at 0–2 °C to 5.97 ± 0.01 cm °C−1 at 2–4.5 °C (Extended Data Fig. 7). Better constraining these mechanisms requires targeted observational campaigns integrating multiple data sources (for example, surface, basal and dynamic mass losses12,13,18) with laboratory-based measurements39 and palaeoclimate records11, alongside comprehensive model evaluation19,40. Where observational constraints remain insufficient, expert surveys can inform prior assumptions41,42.Several key processes remain largely unexplored within ISMIP6, including MICI11, ice–ocean–atmosphere interactions12,43, high-resolution surface mass balance44, ice damage mechanisms45,46 and subglacial hydrology10, which could trigger accelerated AIS mass loss. Their absence from most ISMIP6 simulations excludes them from our uncertainty decomposition. Once incorporated into future experiments, combining our emulation with ISMIP’s systematic design could enable coherent comparisons across these diverse process representations. To realize this potential, transparent and structured documentation of ice-model features is needed to enable robust comparisons. Our feature compilation provides a template for such standardization.We present a machine-learning framework that quantifies cascading AIS uncertainties and enables Bayesian calibration against observations to reduce projection bias. Our observation-constrained projections reveal that higher emissions drive greater AIS mass loss (P ≥ 0.89), directly increasing near-term risk, and that the AIS is committed to twenty-first-century mass loss even under SSP1–1.9 (P ≥ 0.92). Under SSP5–8.5, we identify cascading mechanisms that could drive high-end SLR of 25.4 cm by 2100 (95th percentile; median 15.7 cm), while remaining consistent with satellite observations. Effectively managing these risks requires rapid emissions reductions in line with the Paris Climate Agreement and improved constraints on the primary uncertainty drivers. Ultimately, integrating our framework with systematic model design and targeted observations will enhance Antarctic SLR risk quantification, supporting long-term resilience planning for densely populated coastal communities.MethodsMachine-learning based emulationUnlike computationally expensive numerical ice models that solve complex physical equations, statistical emulators mimic the behaviour of physics-based simulators while remaining computationally efficient50,51. Instead of exactly solving the equations, they learn system behaviour from a comparatively small training set and predict simulation outputs for new scenarios. A robust emulator enables rapid sensitivity analysis, parameter calibration, and derivation of confidence/credible intervals (CIs) with little loss of accuracy50.Training data from numerical modelsWe use ISMIP6-23005,6,7,22,27,52,53,54,55 to prescribe Antarctic SLR contributions over 2015–2100. ISMIP6 provides a framework for quantifying diverse ice-sheet model predictions of AIS evolution under common forcing protocols derived from CMIP5 and CMIP6 AOGCMs6,27. Participating models need only simulate ice shelves and grounding-line evolution, with minimal constraints on other choices27, and thus span the diversity of current ice-sheet modelling capabilities. Together with the systematic experimental design and groups submitting multiple configurations to test individual features, ISMIP6 provides a suitable basis for our emulator5,6.In total, 16 groups with 12 numerical models participated in ISMIP6-2300, groups were encouraged to submit multiple configurations spanning different ice-model parameter combinations, yielding 43 submissions. We excluded IMAU_UFEMISM2 and IMAU_UFEMISM3 as they differ minimally from other IMAU_UFEMISM variants, leaving 41 submissions. Combined with different climate forcing from multiple CMIP models and emissions scenarios, including raw simulations and control runs (no additional forcing since 2015), this gives 340 AIS projections. We use ice thickness variable from each simulation to derive annual SLE contribution by calculating the mass above flotation and applying the conversion factor of 1 mm SLE per 362.5 Gt of ice mass variation5,32.Our emulation and analysis primarily focus on 2015–2100, without extending to 2300, for several reasons. First, the extended ISMIP6-2300 ensemble relies largely on SSP5–8.5 scenario, which is increasingly implausible under current climate policies and nationally determined contributions56,57. Second, it lacks the intermediate scenarios (for example, SSP2–4.5) needed to robustly interpolate the AIS response across a large forcing gap, which can exceed 10 °C between available scenarios by the twenty-third century. Third, emulators trained on the full time series to 2300 reveal the current ensemble cannot robustly capture the strong nonlinearities emerging from the twenty-second century onward (Supplementary Information). The twenty-first century is therefore better suited to robust emulation, as this instability-driven nonlinearity is largely not yet activated, allowing reliable characterization of the uncertainty structure from a limited training set.We selected ice-model features characterizing the high-level physical assumptions in each simulation. Our database comprises 29,240 samples from 340 simulations, each with 86 time steps. For each sample we compiled 21 features (Extended Data Table 1): 18 ice-dynamical features plus the AOGCM, emissions scenario and projection year. Four are numerical (highest spatial resolution, initial year, GMST and projection year) and 17 are categorical. We extracted these from ISMIP6-23005 Tables 1 and 3, supplementary configuration descriptions, review of corresponding original studies and communication with contributors. Following Edwards et al.32, we replaced discrete emissions scenarios with GMST change relative to 2015 for each scenario–AOGCM combination. This accommodates the spread in GMST across AOGCMs under identical scenarios and lets us assess AIS sensitivity to continuous warming rather than to discrete scenario–model pairs. Although we do not include regional climate variables, the inclusion of different CMIP AOGCM options can be considered as a high-level projector to transform GMST to local climate conditions.None of ISMIP6 experiments include MICI, a hypothesized mechanism that could induce rapid ice-shelf collapse through processes such as hydrofracture58 and contribute tens of centimetres of additional mass loss by 210011,24. However, MICI remains speculative and its validity and representation in ice-sheet models are actively debated59,60. Whereas ISMIP6 provides a simplified ice-shelf-collapse scheme (regions with >72.5 mm of annual liquid water for ≥ 10 years are assumed to collapse6,61), it does not capture the full MICI process. Currently, continent-wide MICI has been implemented in only a single model, using forcing profiles distinct from those in ISMIP611, precluding direct integration into our framework. Once MICI experiments are added to ISMIP6, however, our framework can include it as an additional category to study its interactions with other parameters.Emulator algorithm, validation and performanceEmulation of AIS-induced SLE contributions from ice-model features constitutes a supervised regression problem with multi-dimensional feature inputs, continuous scalar output, highly nonlinear relationships, limited sample size and tabular data structure. Given these characteristics, decision-tree ensembles typically outperform neural networks on such data, at lower computational cost and with minimal hyperparameter tuning62,63. We evaluated six algorithms—Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost and a multilayer perceptron—using tenfold cross validation with root-mean-square error (RMSE) as the loss function64,65,66,67. Three hundred forty simulations are split into ten folds: each fold is held out for testing while the other nine train the model, repeated ten times so every simulation is evaluated once. Crucially, we withheld complete time series for whole simulations so each fold represents unseen ice-sheet configurations and tests generalization to new model set-ups. We assessed performance using coefficient of determination (R2), mean absolute error (MAE), RMSE and Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence for evaluating 2100 SLE projection distributions and training time.We constructed a unified emulator spanning all projection years rather than separate year-specific models32, enabling the algorithm to learn continuous temporal relationships between GMST and SLE alongside other forcing variables. Gradient Boosting—which sequentially builds decision trees, each correcting the errors of the previous to capture complex nonlinear relationships—performed best across all metrics, substantially outperforming the multilayer perceptron at faster training speeds (Extended Data Table 2). We therefore adopted Gradient Boosting as our primary emulator.We implement quantile regression to quantify the emulator’s prediction uncertainty68, training two additional emulators targeting the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles to capture 95% CIs, assuming normally distributed emulation errors. Given that our data collection cannot capture all physical processes or implementation details, we incorporate an additional nugget term of 0.1 cm (1σ). This yields uncertainty estimates that adapt to different modelling choices and projection year rather than the uniform, stationary uncertainty of nugget-only approaches. Because decision-tree methods are piecewise constant at leaf nodes and tend to produce temporal discontinuities, we post-processed each projected time series with a Savitzky–Golay filter to preserve temporal correlations. The filter used a 19-year window and first-degree polynomial, with parameters optimized by adding white noise to simulated time series and maximizing recovery of the original signal.The resulting 95% CIs captured 95.5% of true simulation values in tenfold cross validation, demonstrating robust uncertainty quantification (Extended Data Fig. 1). It also captures extreme outcomes, including SLE above 40 cm and below −10 cm. The few uncovered cases occur mostly at small SLE magnitudes, where absolute errors stay generally below 1.5 cm, indicating that the emulator maintains high accuracy across the full range of projected outcomes. Performance is similar for full time series: the emulator reproduces the trajectory and magnitude of SLE projections across diverse, unseen model configurations with only minor errors (Extended Data Fig. 2).Apart from cross validation, we conducted three additional tests to assess the emulator’s performance on different tasks69. First, we withheld all simulations forced by Representative Concentration Pathways 2.6 (n = 41, out of 340) or SSP1–2.6 (n = 27) to test whether the emulator, trained predominantly on high-emissions scenarios and control runs, can predict AIS response to lower GMST trajectories, yielding R2 of 0.96, MAE of 0.95 cm, RMSE of 1.38 cm and KL divergence of 0.07 for 2100 SLR projections (Extended Data Fig. 3). Second, we iteratively held out the complete set of ice-shelf collapse experiments paired with each AOGCM (n = 12 each) to test whether emulator captures ice-shelf collapse impacts on future AIS evolution, giving R2 of 0.93, MAE of 1.56 cm, RMSE of 2.34 cm and KL divergence of 0.77. Lastly, we iteratively held out all simulations (n = 6−12) within each of the 41 ISMIP6 submissions (each a unique ice-model configuration) to test emulator’s ability to predict unseen model configurations, mimicking the challenge of designing new experiments. This test is not possible for all submissions because some use unique modelling choices absent from the rest of the ensemble (for example, PICOP70 is used only by PIK_PISM), for which the emulator has no training data. For the 33 testable configurations, this yielded R2 of 0.74, MAE of 3.73 cm, RMSE of 5.65 cm and KL divergence of 0.17.Our emulator outperforms previous emulators on similar cross-validation tests, achieving 0.98 R2 versus 0.78 for a long-short-term-memory-based and 0.54 for a Gaussian-process-based method71. For the more stringent tests, our emulator demonstrates comparable performance (0.74 R2), suggesting that incorporating detailed modelling choices as features improves predictability of simulated AIS evolution. Moreover, although R2, MAE and RMSE degrade with more stringent tests, the emulator still recovers underlying SLR distributions for both 2100 projections and full time series, with minimal systematic bias (low KL divergence; Extended Data Fig. 3). Combined with rapid training (Extended Data Table 2) and fast inference (~30,000 samples/second on a laptop), our emulator enables ensemble-based probabilistic SLR projections. Given the limited ISMIP6 training data, the final emulator was trained using all available data to maximize model robustness for subsequent sensitivity analysis and SLR projections.Probabilistic framework for SLR projectionsThe numerical ice-sheet model for projecting future SLR can be expressed as:$$y(t)=S({\boldsymbol{\Theta }},\phi (t),t)$$
                    (1)
                where y(t) represents the SLR contribution at time t, S denotes the numerical ice-sheet model operator, Θ = θ1, θ2, …, θ19 is a 19-dimensional parameter vector capturing ice-sheet physical processes and modelling assumptions, ϕ(t) represents the time-dependent GMST trajectory and t is the projection time.Without considering observational constraints, AIS projections can be formulated within a Bayesian hierarchical modelling framework72 that decomposes uncertainty quantification into two components:$$p(y(t),\mathbf{\Theta},\phi(t)) \propto \underbrace{p(y(t)\,|\,\mathbf{\Theta},\phi(t))}_{{\mathrm{process}}\,{\mathrm{model}}} \cdot \underbrace{p(\mathbf{\Theta},\phi(t))}_{{\mathrm{parameter}}\,{\mathrm{model}}}$$
                    (2)
                The process model encapsulates deterministic ice-sheet physics through the numerical model S, conditional on parameter configuration Θ and climate forcing ϕ(t). The parameter model p(Θ, ϕ) characterizes prior distributions over ice-sheet parameters and climate forcing scenarios. For example, ISMIP6 ensemble mean and uncertainty represents a parameter model with equal weighting on parameter choices adopted by the groups’ primary submission5,7. However, this samples the parameter space discretely and may be biased towards modelling choices common among participating groups, potentially underrepresenting the full uncertainty.To achieve computational tractability for probabilistic projections, ice-sheet model simulation can be approximated using our machine-learning emulator (E):$$y(t)\approx \hat{y}(t)=E({\boldsymbol{\Theta }},\phi (t),t)+{\epsilon }_{1}({\boldsymbol{\Theta }},\phi (t),t)+{\epsilon }_{2}$$
                    (3)
                where ϵ1(Θ, ϕ(t), t) captures the emulator-predictive uncertainty, which varies as a function of modelling choices and input conditions and ϵ2 is the nugget term. The probability density of future SLR projections conditioned on modelling choices becomes:$$p(\,y(t)| {\boldsymbol{\Theta }},\phi (t))\approx p(\hat{y}(t)| {\boldsymbol{\Theta }},\phi (t))$$
                    (4)
                The computationally efficient emulator allows ensemble sampling of the underlying joint distribution of both the parameter vector Θ and temperature forcing ϕ(t) by sampling alternative parameter model distributions, thereby supporting quantification of both uncertainty and ambiguity in beliefs or alternative physical assumptions and facilitating comprehensive probabilistic projections of future SLR for different analytical purposes3,17,73,74.SLR sensitivity quantificationFeature-variance decomposition and partial-dependence analysisWe investigated temporally varying SLR sensitivity to different modelling choices by perturbing model parameters and quantifying the resulting variance. Specifically, we constructed an ensemble by randomly sampling 10,000 configurations across the 19 ice-modelling features, using a Monte Carlo method with Latin hypercube sampling, to test the impact of specific modelling choices and their interactions with other features. Given the difficulty of assessing the plausibility of different modelling choices32, we adopt a uniform prior that assigns equal probability to each available modelling option:$${\theta }_{i} \sim U(1,{n}_{i}),\quad i=1,2,\ldots ,19$$
                    (5)
                where ~U denotes follows a uniform distribution and ni is the number of available modelling options for the ith feature in the compiled ISMIP6 database (Extended Data Table 1). During this sampling process, all 19 modelling features are treated as categorical (discrete) variables. The only exception is GMST (relative to 2015 level), which for each time step follows:$$\phi (t) \sim U(0,{\phi }_{{\rm{max}}})$$
                    (6)
                where ϕmax is the maximum GMST across the AOGCMs used in ISMIP6, and ϕ(t) = 0 indicates no further warming since 2015, representing a conservative estimate for the lower bound of GMST variation. We assume independence among modelling features, as these represent unconstrained methodological choices made by different groups based on scientific judgement and computational resources. We then calculate the expected variance induced by each feature θi through systematic perturbation:$${\mathrm{Var}}_{i}(t)={\mathbb{E}}\left[\,\mathrm{Var}\,\left(\hat{y}(t)| {\theta }_{i}=k,{{\boldsymbol{\Theta }}}_{-i},\phi (t)\right)\right],\quad k=1,2,\ldots ,{n}_{i}$$
                    (7)
                where ϕ(t) represents randomly generated temperature ensembles and Θ−i denotes all features except θi, which remain randomly sampled. For each of 10,000 randomly sampled configurations, we calculate the variance across ni predictions obtained by varying only θi. The expected feature-induced variance is then obtained by averaging these variances across all configurations. The GMST induced variance (Varϕ(t)) is investigated by evaluating 50 equally spaced temperature values between 0 and ϕmax, with each temperature value tested against 10,000 random samples of the other model features.The sum of expected feature-induced variance (Varsum(t)) at each time step is then calculated as:$${\text{Var}}_{{\rm{sum}}}(t)=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i=1}^{19}{\text{Var}}_{i}(t)+{\text{Var}}_{\phi }(t)$$
                    (8)
                where Varϕ(t) represents variance related to GMST change. Our variance decomposition is neither ANOVA75 nor Sobol analysis76. Instead, we calculate the expected feature-induced variance for each modelling feature and report variance fractions relative to Varsum(t)—the sum of all expected feature-induced variances—rather than relative to total variance from a full factorial analysis. This method captures interaction effects through ensemble sampling while using additive variance to streamline the analysis, providing a simplified yet efficient framework to quantify each feature’s primary variance contribution and its interactions with other modelling choices. Although Varsum(t) does not strictly follow the law of total variance, it closely approximates the total variance across 10,000 ice-sheet configurations in this case (Supplementary Information).Partial-dependence analysis quantifies the expected SLR when adopting a specific modelling option, averaged over many combinations of the other features. This approach isolates the systematic effect of individual modelling choices on SLR projections. For each feature option, we calculated the mean response:$${\mu }_{i}(t)={\mathbb{E}}[\hat{y}(t)| {\theta }_{i}=k,{{\boldsymbol{\Theta }}}_{-i},\phi (t)],\quad k=1,2,\ldots ,{n}_{i}$$
                    (9)
                where the expected value (μi(t)) is computed across all 10,000 samples with feature θi fixed at value k while other features remain randomly sampled. This reveals how different feature options shift SLR predictions.We conducted variance decomposition and partial-dependence analyses for raw and drift-corrected simulations6,52. For drift-corrected analysis, we added the standard 0.33 ± 0.16 mm yr−1 correction for the historical AIS mass-loss trend3,7,32, treating its uncertainty as an independent variance component that accumulates linearly over time. We excluded bedrock adjustment from variance analyses, as only two groups performed it (using different methods), precluding meaningful cross-model assessment. We also excluded initialization method and initial year from drift-corrected analysis, as suggested by the original experiment design6,52.SLR sensitivity to GMST and emissions scenariosWe employ an ensemble sampling approach to explore the probability distributions of AIS SLR projections conditioned on GMST and emissions scenarios. As in the variance decomposition, we sample GMST uniformly from 0 to the maximum value of the selected AOGCMs at each year, increasing sample size to 50,000 to better resolve continuous GMST distribution. To move beyond discrete GMST values from individual AOGCMs, we use emissions-scenario-specific GMST distributions from FaIR (Finite amplitude Impulse Response) simple climate model30,49, which generates SSP-dependent GMST distributions similar to those used in IPCC AR6, allowing us to explore climate sensitivity, effective radiative forcing and climate variability conditioned on emissions scenarios. We selected five policy-relevant SSPs: SSP1–1.9, SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP3–7.0 and SSP5–8.5 (refs. 77,78). Although SSP1–1.9 was not used in ISMIP6, its GMST trajectory falls between SSP1–2.6 and no-forcing control runs, within the GMST range of our training ensemble. For each SSP, we combine each of 500 FaIR GMST projections with 1,000 randomly selected ice-model features to propagate scenario-specific uncertainty into SLR projections.Scenario dependence probability calculationScenario dependence is the degree to which projected outcomes are influenced by the choice of emission pathway, often quantified by the statistical significance of inter-scenario differences3. We quantify the probability of twenty-first-century AIS positive-scenario dependence (that is, higher emissions yielding higher SLR) using an ensemble of 20,000 random samples from the parameter distributions described in equation (5), with randomly selected GMST values for SSP1–1.9, SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP3–7.0 and SSP5–8.5. At each time step, we calculate the probability that AIS SLR under higher emissions scenarios (SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP3–7.0, SSP5–8.5) exceeds that under SSP1–1.9, holding the ice-model parameter distribution identical across scenarios to isolate the effect of GMST and preserve correlations within each physical configuration. The resulting time-varying probability reflects the likelihood of positive-scenario dependence.Probabilistic framework with Bayesian calibrationThe Bayesian hierarchical framework can be extended to incorporate observational constraints. In this case, equation (2) becomes:$$\begin{array}{l}p(y(t),\mathbf{\Theta}\,|\,\zeta,\phi(t)) \propto \underbrace{p(\zeta\,|\,\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{t}^{*}),\tau)}_{{\mathrm{data}}\,{\mathrm{model}}} \\ \cdot\, \underbrace{p(y(t)\,|\,\mathbf{\Theta},\phi(t))}_{{\mathrm{process}}\,{\mathrm{model}}} \cdot \underbrace{p(\tau,\mathbf{\Theta},\phi(t))}_{{\mathrm{parameter}}\,{\mathrm{model}}}\end{array}$$
                    (10)
                where an additional data model describes the relationship between latent ice-sheet processes and observations. Here t* denotes the observational period encompassing satellite, in situ instrumental and geological measurements, whereas t represents projection timeframes. The vector Y(t*) represents multiple observational quantities, such as total mass variation, surface velocity fields and palaeoglacial AIS behaviours79. The data model p(ζ∣Y(t*), τ) characterizes the likelihood of observing measurements ζ given latent ice-sheet evolution (Y(t*)), where τ captures observational uncertainties and measurement errors. This enables posterior updating of the ice-sheet parameters Θ to constrain projections with observational evidence.Among observational quantities, total ice mass balance is the most straightforward observation for emulator calibration, we therefore focus on this single constraint. We calibrate the prior SLR projections against total AIS mass observations from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and GRACE Follow-On missions. We use the 2002–2021 AIS mass-loss rate of 158 ± 14 Gt yr−1 (ref. 36) (0.44 ± 0.04 mm yr−1), an average trend with decadal climate variability removed, as ice-sheet models cannot adequately capture such variability. We randomly sample 100,000 parameter combinations from the prior distributions and compare their emulated mass-loss rates against observations through a Gaussian likelihood function:$${\mathscr{ \mathcal L }}({\boldsymbol{\Theta }}| {\zeta }_{r},{\sigma }_{r}^{\,\,2})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2{\rm\pi }{\sigma }_{r}^{\,\,2}}}\exp \left(-\frac{{({\zeta }_{r}-\hat{r}({\boldsymbol{\Theta }},\phi ({t}^{* })))}^{2}}{2{\sigma }_{r}^{\,\,2}}\right)$$
                    (11)
                where \({\mathscr{ \mathcal L }}({\boldsymbol{\Theta }}| {\zeta }_{{\rm{r}}},{\sigma }_{{\rm{r}}}^{\,2})\) denotes the likelihood of ice-model configuration Θ given the observed mean mass-loss rate ζr and variance \({\sigma }_{r}^{2}\). The term \(\hat{r}({\boldsymbol{\Theta }},\phi ({t}^{* }))\) is the emulated 2015–2021 mass-loss rate for model configuration Θ, calculated by fitting a first-order ordinary least squares regression to emulated SLR time series forced by smoothed GMST observations (https://climate.nasa.gov/vital-signs/global-temperature). Combining this likelihood with priors yields posterior probabilities for each parameter combination and corresponding SLR projections.Apart from posterior SLR projections, we provide a posterior high-end scheme, which is helpful for practitioners working with long-lasting critical infrastructure (for example, nuclear power stations)17,80. To achieve this, we generate one million posterior samples forced with SSP5–8.5 GMST distributions and then select the samples that generate the top 1% of SLR projections at 2100. Because these subsamples have been calibrated to observed AIS evolution, these parameter combinations represent plausible cascading physical mechanisms that could lead to high-end SLR projections.

items.title: The super El Niño is cooking coral reefs — can lullabies and probiotics save them?
items.body:
NEWS FEATURE
                    
                        30 September 2026

The super El Niño is cooking coral reefs — can lullabies and probiotics save them?

Researchers are trying everything they can to help coral reefs to survive severe heat stress from climate change, including playing sounds underwater.

James Dinneen

James Dinneen

Coral reefs in the Philippines are still recovering from the last El Niño, even as another one gains strength. Credit: Alex Mustard/Nature Picture Library

It’s peak spawning time for coral in the Caribbean Sea and there’s something new in the water this year. Underwater speakers at several locations are serenading clouds of floating larvae as they search for a place on the reef to permanently settle. Sounds recorded at vibrant reefs — such as the clicks of snapping prawn and the thrum of fish — fill the water at spots where coral reefs are struggling because of high temperatures, pollution and other stresses.This El Niño is set to be the largest on record by a ‘mind-blowing margin’The hope is that these sea songs will lure floating coral larvae into settling on the degraded reefs and help them to recover. This project, run by researchers at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) in Massachusetts, relies on the discovery that coral larvae can sense sound and use it as a cue to follow as they search for a permanent home1.“Healthy reefs are naturally broadcasting sound all over the place,” says Aran Mooney, a marine bioacoustician at WHOI who leads the project. He’s part of a small army of researchers stepping up their efforts to save threatened corals. In addition to playing lullabies to restore damaged reefs, they are implementing other emergency measures, such as moving corals from shallow locations to deeper, cooler water and inoculating reefs with protective microorganisms.The planet’s corals need all the help that they can get. This year’s record-breaking ocean temperatures, resulting from human-caused climate change and a super-strong El Niño brewing in the Pacific Ocean, have spurred fresh alarm about the future of coral reefs. Elevated water temperatures can cause coral bleaching, which happens when the usually richly coloured organisms expel the symbiotic algae that they rely on for nutrients; this can ultimately kill the coral.Researchers test a system in Dominica that plays sounds of a healthy reef to help corals grow.Credit: Dan Mele, ©Woods Hole Oceanographic InstitutionAs of late August, coral bleaching had been observed in corals around Florida, the Pacific coast of Panama and Kiribati in the Central Pacific. The Coral Reef Watch of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration found that, in large swathes of the oceans, the water had reached temperatures that placed corals at risk of bleaching and heat mortality. Temperatures are expected to rise even further in 2027 as the El Niño reaches its full strength, and that will raise the risks for corals.Coral reefs can recover from bleaching and their ability to bounce back has often surprised scientists. But recovery takes time and corals can’t catch a break: this year’s bleaching event comes less than a year after the last global one ended in 2025.“It’s sort of like having COVID, also getting the flu, and at the same time being stressed about your job,” says Amy Apprill, a marine geochemist who leads WHOI’s coral-restoration team. She says that the accumulated stress is likely to make the heat this year and in 2027 even more harmful for corals than previous events.Michael Sweet, a coral biologist at the University of Derby, UK, says that, despite the depressing outlook, many researchers are focusing on what they can do to help. “You swing between almost giving up, to going, ‘I’m going to fight to my dying breath to try and make things a bit better’.”Lost reefsThe twenty-first century has not been kind to coral reefs. Four times since 1998, hot oceans — fuelled by global warming and boosted by El Niño events — have caused corals to bleach worldwide. Those bleaching events have taken a toll. According to a major report by hundreds of scientists published in August2, overall hard coral cover between 2020 and 2024 was 9.5% lower than between 1980 and 2009. Much of the decline occurred during the record heat in 2024, which caused bleaching at nearly all of the world’s reefs, and saw hard coral cover fall by 8.9% compared with 2023, the largest single-year drop so far (see ‘Rough times for reefs’).Source: Ref. 2“What that decline tells us is that the recovery is never enough before that decline happens again,” says report co-author Manuel González-Rivero, a coral researcher at the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS) in Cape Cleveland.Projections beyond this year’s El Niño event also look bleak. “Even under the optimistic models for the future ocean temperature, we expect massive bleaching everywhere” over the next decade, says Giovanni Strona, an ecologist who studies corals at the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre in Ispra, Italy.“By the end of the century, many projections predict almost complete annihilation of coral reefs worldwide,” adds Strona. A 2025 study he co-authored argued that, barring massive increases in funding or some major technological advance, the scale of the problem is now too great for restoration efforts to prevent huge declines3.Ocean temperatures set to break all-time record: what’s next?Coral scientists are unequivocal that the priority for protecting corals must be slashing greenhouse-gas emissions and protecting reefs from local stresses such as overfishing and pollution. Climate models suggest that limiting global warming to 1.5 °C relative to the pre-industrial average would spare some coral reefs from repeat bleaching events4. But in a 2 °C warmer world, nearly all reefs would be subjected to severe bleaching regularly — eventually leading to the corals’ death.Scientists working on coral restoration insist that much can still be saved. “Coral reefs have not crossed a point of no return,” states the report2. However, as the world looks set to overshoot both those temperature thresholds, researchers say that the heat is increasingly challenging reefs’ natural recovery capacity and that more-direct interventions are necessary to keep coral reefs alive.“It flips between being an amazing time to be a coral scientist and a biologist in general and having the opportunity to develop and establish these really cool techniques, against the fact that we have to do it” because corals are in trouble, says Sweet, who studies ways to use the coral microbiome to help reefs.That work includes a growing set of techniques that show promise for helping corals, although difficulties scaling them up and a lack of funding remain persistent issues. Some approaches are relatively low-tech. Long-standing coral-gardening projects, for example, are getting better at breeding corals with improved tolerance to heat and acidity5. Other approaches range from treating corals with microbial cocktails and micronutrients to luring larvae using underwater sounds of a healthy reef.Coral lullabiesFor Mooney, the fact that coral larvae — invertebrates less than one millimetre long — could be sensitive to sound came as a big surprise. In 2012, he and his colleagues were listening for differences in the soundscapes of healthy and degraded reefs near the US Virgin Islands. The Caribbean has seen some of the world’s most-severe declines in coral cover due to rising ocean temperatures and other local pressures, such as overfishing, sediment pollution and disease outbreaks.In 2012, it was well known that fish were attracted to the sounds of a vibrant reef6. And Mooney had found that squid, too, were sensitive to sound7, as were crabs8. It occurred to him that other invertebrates, such as corals and oysters, might also use sonic cues to assess a reef’s state.Mooney and his colleagues began conducting experiments to learn more about how corals might use sound. They found that the larvae were sensitive to sonic cues and settled more often when exposed to the ambient sounds of healthy reefs9.Amy Apprill surveys biodiversity at a coral reef near the US Virgin Islands.Credit: Dan Mele, ©Woods Hole Oceanographic InstitutionThen, in 2022, they began testing whether reef soundscapes might be harnessed to help these ecosystems recover by broadcasting recordings of a vibrant reef in places where the reef had gone silent. The team placed coral larvae of the mustard-yellow stony coral Porites astreoides at degraded reefs in special cups that vibrated to let in sound, but that blocked other sensory information, such as light and chemical cues. The researchers then used underwater speakers to broadcast audio recordings of a healthy reef. They found that larvae exposed to the healthy-reef recordings settled almost twice as often, on average, as did the ones without the sound treatment10. “Oh wow. This actually worked,” says Mooney.

Niche differentiation and functional complementarity between rare and abundant taxa sustain grassland soil bacterial diversity
                        Xiaojuan Zhang 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0002-4111-43301, Long Lv2, Saman Herath3, Jie Yang1 & …Zhuangsheng Tang 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-6397-63081 Show authors

Communications Earth & Environment
                             (2026) Cite this article
                        
                        
                            
                                
    
        
            
            
                
            Save article
            
        
        
            
                View saved research

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

AbstractSoil bacterial communities are central to grassland ecosystem functioning, yet how abundant and rare bacteria taxa differ in ecological strategies, community formation, and environmental responses remains unclear. Here we show, using 278 soil samples from grasslands across China, that these groups have contrasting but complementary ecological roles. Abundant taxa are mainly adapted to nutrient-poor conditions, tolerate a wider range of environments, and are shaped largely by random ecological processes. Rare taxa are more often associated with nutrient-rich conditions, occupy narrower environmental niches, and are governed more strongly by environmental selection. Machine-learning analyses identify pH and aridity index as the main drivers of diversity and community assembly in both groups. Predicted functions also differ: abundant taxa contribute more to carbon fixation, whereas rare taxa play greater roles in nitrogen cycling. Abundant bacterial functions depend mainly on geography and community composition, whereas rare bacterial functions rely more on diversity and respond more strongly to environmental change, highlighting their complementary contributions.

L’intervento del Commissario ARPAT Pietro Rubellini sui segnali più preoccupanti della crisi climatica e sul ruolo strategico del monitoraggio ambientale a supporto delle decisioni pubbliche

Il Commissario ARPAT Pietro Rubellini è intervenuto agli Stati generali dell’ambiente, la manifestazione organizzata da Ricicla TV al Teatro della Compagnia di Firenze, con il patrocinio istituzionale della Regione Toscana, Assessorato all’Ambiente, e la partnership del Ministero dell’ambiente e della sicurezza energetica, di ISPRA e del Sistema nazionale per la protezione dell’ambiente (SNPA).
Il presidente della Toscana Eugenio Giani e l’assessore all’Ambiente della Toscana David Barontini hanno preso parte a questa prima edizione della nuova rassegna, che si concluderà a Napoli nella primavera del 2027.
L’evento ha riunito istituzioni, imprese, mondo della ricerca e comunità locali per confrontarsi sui temi dell’economia circolare, della rigenerazione e tutela del territorio e della transizione energetica, offrendo uno sguardo concreto sulle sfide e le opportunità della transizione ecologica in Toscana.
Nel corso della seconda sessione, “Dalla rigenerazione alla tutela del territorio. Parchi, biodiversità e paesaggio: il valore del capitale naturale toscano”, il Commissario ARPAT Pietro Rubellini ha risposto alle domande di Monica D’Ambrosio, direttrice di Ricicla TV, sui cambiamenti climatici che stanno alterando parametri e standard di riferimento per il monitoraggio ambientale. In particolare, ha evidenziato i fenomeni che destano maggiore preoccupazione e l’importanza di tradurre i dati ambientali in decisioni sempre più efficaci per la tutela del territorio.
Tra gli effetti più evidenti dei cambiamenti climatici, Pietro Rubellini richiama la trasformazione del clima mediterraneo, caratterizzata da estati sempre più calde e da un regime delle precipitazioni profondamente modificato. Negli ultimi dieci anni sono infatti aumentati gli eventi piovosi intensi e di breve durata, le cosiddette “bombe d’acqua”, che oltre a provocare alluvioni e frane producono conseguenze non solo quantitative ma anche qualitative su molti comparti ambientali.
Fra le criticità più preoccupanti vi sono le difficoltà dei sistemi di raccolta e depurazione delle acque reflue, progettati in un contesto climatico diverso da quello attuale. Durante gli eventi meteorici più intensi, infatti, gli impianti possono andare in sofferenza e parte delle acque viene convogliata direttamente nei corpi idrici superficiali, con ripercussioni sulla qualità di fiumi e acque costiere e possibili divieti temporanei di balneazione.
Un secondo segnale – ha sottolineato Rubellini rivolgendosi in particolare alla platea degli studenti presenti in sala – riguarda le acque sotterranee. Le precipitazioni sempre più brevi e concentrate, che non consentono all’acqua di infiltrarsi adeguatamente nel sottosuolo, riducono la capacità di ricarica delle falde, alterandone l’equilibrio e favorendo, nelle aree costiere, l’intrusione di acqua salata, attraverso il cosiddetto cuneo salino. Quest’acqua, poi pompata in superficie, provoca una progressiva salinizzazione del suolo, compromettendone in prospettiva la capacità di coltivazione e, di conseguenza, la sua produttività.
Trasformare i dati ambientali in decisioni efficaci – ha precisato Rubellini- significa prima di tutto rafforzare la conoscenza e la consapevolezza della cittadinanza. In un contesto in cui informazioni scorrette e semplificazioni rischiano di ostacolare scelte fondate su evidenze scientifiche, le agenzie tecnico-scientifiche, come ARPAT, sono chiamate non solo a fornire dati ai decisori politici, ma anche a costruire un solido substrato di conoscenza nei cittadini e nelle cittadine, che consenta loro di valutare con consapevolezza, senza cadere in strumentalizzazioni, e permettere ai decisori di assumere decisioni sapendo che saranno comprese e valutate all’interno di un dibattito democratico, al riparo dalle distorsioni dell’ignoranza.
Guardando al futuro, Rubellini immagina una Toscana capace di coniugare salute degli ecosistemi, qualità della vita e sviluppo sostenibile. Le priorità indicate sono la riduzione della dipendenza dai combustibili fossili per la produzione di energia e il superamento di un’agricoltura ad alto impiego di prodotti chimici di sintesi.
In questo percorso assume un ruolo importante anche la partecipazione di ARPAT all’Osservatorio nazionale sull’adattamento climatico, che ha il compito di accompagnare l’attuazione del Piano nazionale di adattamento ai cambiamenti climatici. Attraverso il contributo dei propri esperti, l’Agenzia mette a disposizione dati, monitoraggi e competenze maturate sul territorio toscano per trasformare le conoscenze scientifiche in strategie e azioni concrete di adattamento.
